mcqs.question: You're picking a VM instance family for an in-memory cache that needs very little CPU but a huge amount of RAM. What ratio should you look for?
options: A memory-optimized instance with a high memory-per-vCPU ratio
A compute-optimized instance with a low memory-per-vCPU ratio
It doesn't matter, all instance families offer the same ratio
A general-purpose instance is always the safest default
mcqs.explanation: A cache is memory-bound, not CPU-bound, so you want an instance family with a high GB-per-vCPU ratio — a memory-optimized family. A compute-optimized instance would waste money on CPU you don't need while potentially starving on RAM.

mcqs.question: A nightly batch job processes a large dataset, checkpoints progress every few minutes, and can resume from the last checkpoint if interrupted. Which pricing model fits best?
options: Reserved instances, to lock in a long-term discount
Spot/preemptible instances, since the job tolerates interruption and this is the cheapest option
On-demand, since batch jobs can't tolerate any interruption
None of these apply to batch workloads
mcqs.explanation: Spot instances offer the deepest discount specifically because they can be reclaimed with little warning — a perfect fit for a job designed to checkpoint and resume. Reserved makes sense for steady, always-on load, not a nightly job.

mcqs.question: Your database needs fast, consistent random read/write I/O and is only ever accessed by the one VM it runs on. Which storage type is the right fit?
options: Object storage, for its unlimited scale
File storage, for its shared access across clients
Block storage, attached directly to that VM
Any of the three work equally well here
mcqs.explanation: Block storage is built exactly for this pattern: low-latency random I/O for a single attached VM, which is what a database engine needs. Object storage adds network/API overhead per operation, and file storage's shared-access model isn't the right shape here.

mcqs.question: A storage service advertises 11 nines of durability but only 99.9% availability. What does this actually guarantee?
options: Your data will never be lost, and it will always be instantly reachable
These two numbers measure the same thing, just expressed differently
Your data can be lost occasionally, but it's always reachable when present
Your data is extremely unlikely to be lost, but the service can still have brief periods where it's unreachable
mcqs.explanation: Durability and availability answer different questions: durability is about data survival over time, availability is about whether you can reach it right now. High durability with imperfect availability means your data is safe but might be briefly unreachable.
